nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun powers the seagrass, algae and phytoplankton of the shallow lagoon, and the algae living inside reef corals.

nodes.name: Warm lagoon water
nodes.desc: The enclosed lagoon is shallow, averaging about 25 m deep, and warm and clear enough for reef corals and seagrass to thrive.

nodes.name: Ocean passages
nodes.desc: Natural gaps in the barrier reef, such as the Boulari passage, let ocean water flow into and out of the lagoon.

nodes.name: River silt and nutrients
nodes.desc: Rivers carry soil into the lagoon. Mangroves trap some of it, but heavy runoff from mining and grazing has buried reefs in silt.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, mangrove leaves and animals, returning nutrients to the sediment.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: Low seagrass meadows in the shallow lagoon, the main food of dugongs and adult green turtles.

nodes.name: Mangroves
nodes.desc: Mangrove forests fringe the shore and help retain sediment before it reaches the reef.

nodes.name: Reef algae
nodes.desc: Algae growing on reef rock and sand, grazed by parrotfish and surgeonfish.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae that feed zooplankton and corals. General ecological knowledge.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults graze mostly seagrass, nibbling blade tops so beds stay healthy. The lagoon is an important nesting site.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: Feeds mainly on seagrass. New Caledonia holds the third largest dugong population in the world, and hunting is banned there.

nodes.name: Parrotfish
nodes.desc: Most species scrape algae from reef rock with their beaks, which keeps algae from overgrowing the reef.

nodes.name: Surgeonfish
nodes.desc: Reef fish that graze algae. General ecological knowledge for the family.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting crustaceans that graze phytoplankton and feed many reef animals.

nodes.name: Reef-building corals
nodes.desc: Branching and table corals build the reef structure. The lagoon coral diversity matches or exceeds the Great Barrier Reef.

nodes.name: Common coral trout
nodes.desc: An ambush predator of the reef that eats mainly fish, including parrotfish. Caught here by line and spear.

nodes.name: Lipspot moray
nodes.desc: A small moray eel living in reef crevices, and the main prey of the New Caledonian sea krait.

nodes.name: Yellow-lipped sea krait
nodes.desc: A sea snake endemic to New Caledonia that hunts mostly eel-like fishes, about half of them lipspot morays.

nodes.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
nodes.desc: Eats living hard coral, especially Acropora, leaving white skeleton. Outbreaks can devastate reefs.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: Wide-ranging predator that eats turtles, dugongs, fish and sea snakes, and also scavenges carcasses.

nodes.name: Grey reef shark
nodes.desc: A reef shark that hunts reef fish. The lagoons hold healthy populations of top predators.
